comparison: Perfect alignment on heart findings (C69-C77). Both evaluations support that TFAM modulation has no effect in heart tissue due to endogenous TFAM upregulation representing a maximally engaged compensatory mechanism. OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the data quality and interpretation.

Perfect alignment on colon findings (C78-C85). Both evaluations support the negative effects of TFAM overexpression in colon, paralleling liver responses. Reviewers accept this as part of the comprehensive tissue-specific pattern with no challenges to the data or interpretation.

Perfect alignment on BAT findings (C86-C92). Both evaluations support the unexpected beneficial effect of TFAM reduction in brown adipose tissue. Peer reviewer explicitly affirms 'reduced TFAM levels improve brown adipocyte tissue function,' matching OpenEval's assessment.

Perfect alignment on spleen findings (C93-C105). Both evaluations support beneficial effects of TFAM overexpression in spleen. Peer reviewer explicitly states 'increased TFAM levels increase mtDNA copy number in the spleen and improve spleen homeostasis,' directly confirming OpenEval's assessment.

Perfect alignment on mtDNA mutator model characteristics (C42-C43). Both evaluations accept this as established background information about the model, supported by prior citations. No challenges from either evaluation.

Strong alignment on background/established knowledge (C1-C3, C8-C30, C108-C111). Both evaluations support these foundational claims. OpenEval notes extensive citations to prior literature; peer reviewers implicitly accept the scientific context without challenge. Minor difference: peer R11 excludes C108-C111 which appear in peer R14.

Strong alignment on liver findings (C50-C68). Both evaluations support the detrimental effects of TFAM overexpression in liver. Peer reviewer explicitly affirms 'increased TFAM levels...do not elevate mtDNA copy number in the liver and impair mtDNA expression.' OpenEval provides more detailed mechanistic interpretation including FGF21 stress markers.

Strong alignment on body weight and organ-to-body weight ratios (C36-C38, C41). Both evaluations support these phenotypic observations without challenge. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through endorsement of overall data quality. OpenEval R1 also covers testis rescue (C39-C40) not included in peer R3.

Strong alignment on main conclusions about tissue-specific effects (C4-C6, C106-C107, C112). Both evaluations strongly support these core findings. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm 'TFAM's counteractive role in mtDNA mutator mice is tissue-specific' with 'convincing evidence,' matching OpenEval's comprehensive assessment.

Alignment on TFAM-to-mtDNA ratio data (C47-C49). Both evaluations support these calculated ratios as providing mechanistic insight. Peer reviewers affirm the quality and interpretation; OpenEval notes the data derive from TFAM protein (n=2) and mtDNA levels (n≥5).

Alignment on tissue-specific mtDNA responses (C44-C46). Both evaluations support that TFAM overexpression fails to increase mtDNA in liver/heart but does in BAT/spleen. OpenEval R2 also covers C31-C32 not in peer R5. Both accept the tissue-specific pattern.

Alignment on testis rescue effect (C39-C40). Both evaluations support this finding. Peer reviewers accept it alongside spleen as examples of beneficial TFAM effects. OpenEval R1 covers broader phenotypic data (C36-C41) while peer R4 focuses specifically on testis/spleen rescue.

Alignment on model characterization and comparative discussion (C117-C121). Both evaluations support these mechanistic explanations. OpenEval finds the inference about more severe pathology reasonable; peer reviewers do not challenge the model characterization, with concerns resolved in revision.

Alignment on stress markers and OXPHOS dysfunction (C54, C57, C63). Both evaluations support these mechanistic interpretations based on cited prior work. OpenEval notes these are appropriately cited background facts; peer reviewers accept as well-established consequences.

Alignment on conclusion that other factors beyond TFAM are involved (C7, C113). Both evaluations support this inference. Peer reviewer explicitly states authors conclude 'there must be other determinants of mtDNA copy number,' treating as valid. OpenEval finds it reasonable given unexpected responses.

Alignment on speculative interpretations about additional factors (C122-C124). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these are speculative but reasonable discussion points lacking direct validation. Peer reviewers accept as appropriately framed speculation, with R15 noting these align with supported main conclusions.

Alignment on breeding scheme and maternal transmission (C115-C116). Both evaluations support the experimental design. OpenEval notes this ensures wild-type mtDNA transmission; peer reviewers accept methodology with concerns resolved in revision.

Alignment on therapeutic implications (C114). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting this represents hypothesis rather than demonstrated result. Peer reviewers accept the translational discussion as reasonable given the data, with R14 affirming 'the need for nuanced approaches when targeting TFAM for therapeutic interventions.'

Partial alignment on mtDNA copy number findings (C31-C32). Both evaluations support tissue-specific mtDNA responses. OpenEval R2 focuses on qPCR data showing differential responses; peer R1 incorporates these as part of broader tissue-specific conclusion with additional claims.

Partial alignment on stress markers (C54-C57, C63). OpenEval R4 covers these within comprehensive liver analysis (C50-C68); peer R13 groups them separately as mechanistic interpretations. Both evaluations support these claims based on established knowledge and current data.

Partial alignment on discussion/implications (C108-C111). Both evaluations support these interpretive claims. OpenEval R14 groups with extensive background (C1-C30); peer R14 focuses on discussion/significance claims including therapeutic implications (C114). Both find claims reasonable.
